title: Patterns of Reasoning
short: Arguments reason from examples (induction), from general principles (deduction), from cause and effect, from comparison and from analogy.
trouble: Learners can’t say how an argument gets from its evidence to its claim, so they can’t judge whether the step is strong.

blocks.html: Once you know your claim, you need a way to get there from your evidence. The Logic Ladder separates deductive and inductive arguments. Writers use a handful of common patterns built on those two.

head: Pattern
How it reasons
Example
Test it by asking
rows: Examples (induction)
from several cases to a general claim
Three schools that added a later start saw attendance rise, so later starts tend to help attendance.
Are there enough cases? Are they typical?
Principle (deduction)
from a general rule to this case
Every club must have a faculty sponsor; the chess club has none, so it can’t be approved yet.
Is the rule true? Does this case fall under it?
Cause and effect
from a cause to its result, or back
The broken streetlight leaves the corner dark, so drivers can’t see walkers there.
Is there another cause? Does the cause come first?
Comparison
from a similar case of the same kind
The next town’s evening swim lessons filled up, so ours would too.
Are the two cases alike in the ways that matter?
Analogy
from a different kind of thing that shares a feature
A school without a library is like a kitchen without a pantry.
Does the shared feature matter for the claim?
blocks.cap: Five patterns of reasoning. Textbooks group them a little differently; the tests are what matter.

blocks.html: Every argument moves from evidence to claim by some pattern: examples, a principle, cause and effect, comparison or analogy. Name the pattern, then apply its test.

Each pattern can fail in its own way. Examples can be too few (a hasty generalization), a cause can be mistaken (false cause), an analogy can rest on a likeness that doesn’t matter (weak analogy). Knowing the pattern tells you which question will expose a weak step, in your argument or anyone else’s.

blocks.title: An analogy in the Federalist
blocks.q: Madison, Federalist No. 10: “Liberty is to faction what air is to fire, an aliment without which it instantly expires.” What pattern is this, and does it hold up?
steps: It compares two different kinds of things: liberty and air, faction and fire. That is an analogy.
The shared feature: each feeds the other. Without air, fire dies; without liberty, factions (groups pursuing their own interests) can’t form.
The point Madison draws: removing liberty would end faction, but that cure is worse than the disease, just as removing air to stop fire would kill everything that breathes.
The analogy holds where the feature matters: both cures destroy something essential.
blocks.a: An analogy, used to show why removing liberty is the wrong cure for faction.

blocks.title: Name the pattern
blocks.q: “Since we added a bike rack by the front door, twice as many students ride to school.” What pattern is this, and what should a skeptic ask?
steps: It claims the rack caused more riding: cause and effect.
Test: did anything else change? Maybe a new bike lane opened, or the weather was better this year.
A stronger version would compare with a school that didn’t add a rack.
blocks.a: Cause and effect. Ask what else changed at the same time.

blocks.html: Not being able to say how an argument gets from its evidence to its claim. If you can’t name the step, you can’t judge it, and neither can your reader. Check: after each piece of evidence, finish the sentence “This supports my claim because …” and name the pattern you are using.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Our last three bake sales each raised over \$300, so bake sales are a reliable fundraiser for us.
All library books are due in three weeks, so this one is due on the 14th.
The creek floods because the storm drains upstream are clogged with leaves.
Learning to write without revising is like learning to cook without tasting.
Players who skip warm-ups pull muscles more often, so skipping warm-ups leads to injuries.
Every member must pay dues to vote, and Kai hasn’t paid, so he can’t vote yet.
